patient.name: Gareth Hughes
patient.complaint: Keeps clipping his wing mirrors and bumping into people on both sides

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely finding on visual field testing?' or 'Which is the most likely site of the lesion?': map the defect to its level (optic nerve, chiasm, tract, temporal or parietal radiation, occipital cortex).

points: Gareth, 54, a bus driver, keeps **clipping wing mirrors on both sides**.
People 'appear out of nowhere' at his sides.
Reading and central vision feel normal.

steps.lead: Gareth's pattern of lost vision will tell us **where** along the pathway the lesion sits.
Stroke, tumour and MS are the big causes; in a 54 year old with headache and low libido, think **tumour**.

points: Each eye has lost its temporal field; nasal fields intact.

steps.q: Gareth has lost the temporal field in both eyes. Where is the lesion?
steps.r: **Bitemporal hemianopia** = the **chiasm**, where the nasal fibres from both eyes cross. Classically a pituitary adenoma.

visual.title: Where along the visual pathway?
visual.label: Gareth: chiasm
visual.caption: Front of the pathway = one eye; chiasm = both temporal fields; behind the chiasm = homonymous.

steps.lead: Gareth's defect is the chiasmal one. Learn the others by level, because the exam gives you the defect and asks for the site.

steps.text: **PITS**: **P**arietal = **I**nferior, **T**emporal = **S**uperior. 'Pie in the sky' is temporal; 'pie on the floor' is parietal.

steps.lead: Gareth's central vision is fine, but the occipital signature is **macular sparing** in a homonymous hemianopia.
Gareth's upper temporal quadrants went first: pressure from **below** the chiasm, typical of a **pituitary** tumour.

steps.text: A **sudden** homonymous hemianopia is a **stroke** (often posterior circulation) until proven otherwise: an emergency, not a clinic referral.

steps.lead: Gareth's job depends on his fields: delay risks **permanent** vision loss and his livelihood.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (confrontation, then formal perimetry) or 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (MRI brain, or pituitary MRI for a bitemporal defect).

steps.lead: Gareth's defect was found with bedside **confrontation**; **formal perimetry** then maps it precisely.

visual.title: Gareth's perimetry: mean deviation
visual.label: Gareth −9 dB
visual.caption: Moderate field loss in both eyes, densest in the upper temporal quadrants.

steps.q: Which test best shows the cause of Gareth's bitemporal hemianopia?
steps.r: **MRI brain** is the gold standard to characterise the lesion, here a pituitary MRI.

steps.lead: Gareth's **MRI** shows a 2.8 cm **pituitary macroadenoma** lifting and compressing the chiasm.

steps.title: Gareth's pituitary bloods
steps.text: Mildly raised prolactin (stalk compression) with low gonadotrophins and secondary hypothyroidism: a **non-functioning** macroadenoma.
A prolactin only **mildly** raised with a big tumour is **stalk compression**, not a prolactinoma. Very high levels (thousands) suggest prolactinoma.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' where the cause decides: trans-sphenoidal surgery for a compressive pituitary adenoma, surgery for other tumours, and the stroke pathway for a sudden homonymous hemianopia.

steps.q: Gareth has a non-functioning macroadenoma compressing the chiasm. What is definitive treatment?
steps.r: A compressive macroadenoma with a field defect needs **trans-sphenoidal surgery**. Cabergoline is for prolactinomas.

steps.lead: Gareth has **trans-sphenoidal surgery**; his thyroid and testosterone are replaced and cortisol is covered peri-operatively.

visual.title: Gareth's visual fields after surgery
visual.caption: Fields improve once the chiasm is decompressed; long-standing compression may not fully recover.

steps.title: Treat the cause
nodes: Map the defect: site of lesion
MRI brain to find the cause

steps.lead: Untreated, Gareth's fields would keep shrinking: **permanent** loss and a poorer quality of life.

steps.text: Gareth must tell the **DVLA**. Bus and lorry drivers have stricter field standards; a homonymous or bitemporal defect usually stops driving until fields recover.

steps.lead: Had Gareth's hemianopia come on **suddenly**, he would follow the **NICE stroke pathway**: urgent CT and thrombolysis or thrombectomy if eligible.

science.exam: Expect applied questions on the anatomy: why a chiasmal lesion is bitemporal, why lesions behind the chiasm are homonymous, Meyer's loop, and macular sparing.

steps.lead: Gareth's tumour sits at the **chiasm**, the one point where fibres from both eyes meet.
The crossing **nasal** fibres carry the **temporal** fields, so squashing Gareth's chiasm took out both temporal fields.
Behind the chiasm each tract carries the **same half** of both eyes' fields, so lesions there are **homonymous**.

steps.q: A right temporal lobe tumour damages Meyer's loop. Which defect results?
steps.r: Meyer's loop carries the **superior** field; a **right** lesion affects the **left** field: **left superior quadrantanopia**.

steps.lead: Temporal fibres (Meyer's loop) dip low and carry the upper field; parietal fibres carry the lower field.
The occipital pole's **dual supply** (PCA plus MCA collaterals) is why macular vision often survives a PCA infarct.

mcq.q: Which field defect does a pituitary adenoma compressing the chiasm cause?
Which defect follows an optic nerve lesion?
mcq.r: Before the chiasm only **one eye** is affected.

mcq.q: A temporal lobe lesion causes which defect?
Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing localises to which site?
A lower bitemporal defect worse than upper suggests which tumour?
mcq.r: Compression from **above**: craniopharyngioma, often with diabetes insipidus.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard imaging for a visual field defect?
What maps a visual field defect precisely?
How is bitemporal hemianopia from a pituitary adenoma treated?
A sudden homonymous hemianopia should be managed as what?
mcq.r: Sudden homonymous hemianopia = posterior circulation **stroke** until proven otherwise.

mcq.q: Which fibres cross at the optic chiasm?
mcq.r: **Nasal** fibres carry the temporal fields and decussate.

technique.stem: A 71 year old man with atrial fibrillation noticed yesterday that he keeps missing objects on his right side. He has no limb weakness or speech problem. Visual field testing shows a right homonymous hemianopia with sparing of central vision.
technique.q: Which is the most likely site of the lesion?

steps.x: A site question: level first, then side.
Homonymous = behind the chiasm; **macular sparing** = occipital; right field = **left** brain.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Left occipital cortex** (left PCA infarct, likely embolic from AF).

elim: Gives monocular loss, not a homonymous defect.
Gives a right **inferior** quadrantanopia, often with other parietal signs.

steps.x: **A. Left occipital cortex.** Homonymous + macular sparing = contralateral occipital cortex.

technique.stem: A 60 year old woman tells her GP she keeps walking into door frames on her left. Acuity is 6/9 in both eyes and fundoscopy is normal. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial assessment of her vision?

steps.x: Initial assessment: the bedside test first.

clues: walking into door frames on her left
steps.x: Suspected **left-sided field defect**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bedside **confrontation testing**, then formal perimetry.

elim: Imaging comes after the defect is confirmed (unless acute stroke).
Gold standard for the cause, not the initial assessment.
Images the retina and optic nerve head, not the field.

steps.x: **E. Visual field confrontation testing.** Field defect: confrontation first, perimetry next, MRI for the cause.

technique.stem: A 48 year old woman has a bitemporal hemianopia. MRI shows a 2.5 cm pituitary macroadenoma compressing the optic chiasm. Her prolactin is only mildly raised. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?

steps.x: Definitive management: treat the cause of the defect.

clues: pituitary macroadenoma compressing the optic chiasm
steps.x: Non-functioning macroadenoma (stalk effect), chiasm compressed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Trans-sphenoidal surgery**.

elim: Dopamine agonists shrink prolactinomas; a mild rise is stalk compression.
A field defect means it needs decompression.
Rehabilitation aid, not treatment of the cause.

steps.x: **E. Trans-sphenoidal surgery.** Pituitary adenoma with bitemporal hemianopia = trans-sphenoidal surgery.

technique.stem: A 35 year old man has a tumour in his left temporal lobe. Visual field testing shows a right superior quadrantanopia. A student asks why the upper field is affected.
technique.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Compression of the optic chiasm from below
Damage to the superior optic radiation
Loss of dual blood supply to the macula

steps.x: A mechanism question about a quadrantanopia.
Temporal lobe lesion, **superior** contralateral quadrant: 'pie in the sky'.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Meyer's loop** (inferior radiation in the temporal lobe) carries the superior field.
**B. Damage to Meyer's loop.** PITS: temporal = superior, through Meyer's loop.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman has 9 months of headaches and irregular periods. She has had two near misses while driving because cars seemed to appear from the sides. Acuity is 6/6 in both eyes. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on visual field testing?
practice.e: A pituitary adenoma compresses the crossing nasal fibres at the chiasm, giving bitemporal hemianopia; drivers miss objects on both sides.

steps.x: A finding question: guess the lesion first.

clues: cars seemed to appear from the sides
steps.x: Endocrine upset plus loss of both side fields: **pituitary** tumour at the chiasm.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bitemporal hemianopia**.

elim: A right-sided lesion behind the chiasm; affects one side only.
Slow, with raised pressure and cupped discs; no endocrine features.

steps.x: **A. Bitemporal hemianopia.** Pituitary + both sides missing = bitemporal hemianopia.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man had a right temporal lobe haemorrhage 2 months ago. He now complains that he misses objects in the upper left part of his vision. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 146/88 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on visual field testing?
practice.e: Meyer's loop in the right temporal lobe carries the left superior field, so the defect is a left superior quadrantanopia.

steps.x: A finding question: lobe gives the quadrant, side gives the field.

clues: upper left part of his vision
steps.x: Temporal = **superior**, right lesion = **left** field.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Left superior quadrantanopia** ('pie in the sky').
**C. Left superior quadrantanopia.** PITS: temporal = superior, contralateral.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman has a left parietal glioma. She has difficulty reading and seeing steps below her on the right. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 132/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely visual field defect?
practice.e: The superior optic radiation in the parietal lobe carries the inferior field, so a left parietal lesion causes a right inferior quadrantanopia.

steps.x: A finding question: parietal lobe, which quadrant?

clues: seeing steps below her on the right
steps.x: Parietal = **inferior**; left lesion = **right** field.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Right inferior quadrantanopia** ('pie on the floor').
**C. Right inferior quadrantanopia.** PITS: parietal = inferior, contralateral.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman has 3 days of blurred vision in her left eye with pain on moving the eye. Colours look washed out. The right eye is normal. She had tingling in her legs a year ago. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely visual field defect?
practice.e: An optic nerve lesion such as optic neuritis is before the chiasm, so only one eye loses vision, typically centrally with colour desaturation.

steps.x: A finding question: one eye or both?

clues: blurred vision in her left eye
steps.x: Painful monocular loss with colour desaturation, past sensory symptoms: **optic neuritis** (MS).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Optic nerve lesion: **monocular** (central) vision loss.

elim: Behind the chiasm; affects both eyes.
Behind the chiasm; affects both eyes.

steps.x: **C. Left monocular central loss.** Pre-chiasm lesion = one eye only.

practice.stem: A 10 year old boy has headaches, is the shortest in his class and has started drinking and passing large volumes of water. Visual fields show a bitemporal defect affecting the lower quadrants more than the upper.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his visual field defect?
practice.e: Lower quadrant bitemporal loss means compression of the chiasm from above, commonly a craniopharyngioma, which is associated with diabetes insipidus.

steps.x: A cause question: which way is the chiasm pressed?

clues: lower quadrants more than the upper
steps.x: Lower > upper = compression from **above**; diabetes insipidus and short stature in a child.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Craniopharyngioma**.
**A. Craniopharyngioma.** Lower bitemporal + DI = craniopharyngioma.

practice.stem: A 76 year old man has sudden weakness of his left arm and face. His pulse is irregularly irregular. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 168/94 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: ECG
visual.caption: Atrial fibrillation: irregularly irregular, no P waves.

practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on visual field testing?
practice.e: A right hemisphere stroke affecting the optic tract or radiation gives a left homonymous hemianopia, on the same side as the left-sided weakness. AF is the embolic source.

steps.x: A finding question: which side is the lesion?

clues: sudden weakness of his left arm and face
steps.x: AF with embolic **right hemisphere** stroke (left-sided weakness).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Left homonymous hemianopia**, the same side as the weakness.

elim: Optic nerve or retinal artery, one eye.

steps.x: **B. Left homonymous hemianopia.** Hemianopia is on the same side as the paresis.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman has a possible right-sided field defect on confrontation testing. Her GP wants the defect mapped accurately before imaging. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to map the defect?
practice.e: Bedside confrontation is the initial test, and formal perimetry maps the defect precisely; MRI then characterises the lesion.

steps.x: Investigation to map the field, not find the cause.

clues: possible right-sided field defect on confrontation testing
steps.x: Confrontation done; now quantify.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Formal perimetry**.

elim: Looks for the cause, not the field shape.
Tests conduction, not the field map.

steps.x: **B. Formal perimetry.** Confrontation then perimetry.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man has a bitemporal hemianopia on perimetry. He has reduced libido. His pulse rate is 66 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: MRI brain is the gold standard to characterise the lesion causing a field defect; for bitemporal hemianopia it shows the pituitary and chiasm.

steps.x: Diagnostic investigation for the cause.
Chiasmal lesion with hypogonadism: **pituitary adenoma**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MRI brain** (pituitary protocol), the gold standard.

elim: Less detail of the sella and chiasm.

steps.x: **C. MRI brain (pituitary).** Field defect cause = MRI brain.

practice.stem: A 12 year old girl has a lower bitemporal hemianopia and polyuria. MRI shows a suprasellar craniopharyngioma pressing on the optic chiasm from above. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management of the cause of her field defect?
practice.e: Field defects from tumours are managed by treating the cause, here surgical resection of the craniopharyngioma, to prevent permanent visual loss.

steps.x: Definitive management of the cause.

clues: craniopharyngioma pressing on the optic chiasm
steps.x: Compressive tumour from above.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Surgical resection**; treat the underlying cause.

elim: Ongoing compression risks permanent visual loss.

steps.x: **D. Surgical resection.** Tumour causing a field defect = surgery.

practice.stem: A 69 year old woman has a sudden right homonymous hemianopia that began 2 hours ago. CT head shows no haemorrhage. She has no contraindications. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 162/90 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Sudden homonymous hemianopia is a posterior circulation stroke until proven otherwise; within 4.5 hours with no haemorrhage, the stroke pathway gives IV thrombolysis.

steps.x: Initial management of sudden homonymous hemianopia.
Acute ischaemic (posterior circulation) stroke within 4.5 hours.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stroke pathway: **IV thrombolysis**.

elim: For giant cell arteritis or optic neuritis, not stroke.

steps.x: **A. Intravenous alteplase.** Sudden homonymous hemianopia = stroke pathway.

practice.stem: A 61 year old taxi driver has a permanent left homonymous hemianopia after a stroke 3 months ago. He wants to return to work. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: He can drive if he turns his head more
He must inform the DVLA and not drive
Wear prism glasses and continue driving
practice.e: Homonymous hemianopia usually means the patient fails the DVLA visual field standard, so he must inform the DVLA and not drive; this is part of its impact on quality of life.

steps.x: Advice about a consequence of a field defect.
A homonymous hemianopia usually fails the **DVLA** field standard.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Inform the **DVLA** and stop driving.

elim: Daylight does not fix the field loss.
Compensation does not meet the standard.
Prisms do not meet the legal standard.

steps.x: **C. He must inform the DVLA and not drive.** Field defect + driving = tell the DVLA.

practice.stem: A 50 year old man has a pituitary macroadenoma growing upwards into the optic chiasm. He has lost the temporal half of the visual field in each eye. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for this pattern?
o: Optic tract damage on one side
Pressure on crossing nasal retinal fibres
practice.e: Nasal retinal fibres carry the temporal field and decussate at the chiasm, so a pituitary tumour pressing there removes both temporal fields.

steps.x: A mechanism question: which fibres are hit at the chiasm?

clues: growing upwards into the optic chiasm
temporal half of the visual field in each eye
steps.x: Chiasm lesion with **bitemporal** loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The **nasal** retinal fibres carry the temporal field and **cross** at the chiasm.

elim: These do not cross and carry the nasal field.

steps.x: **E. Pressure on crossing nasal retinal fibres.** Bitemporal = crossing nasal fibres at the chiasm.

prompts.q: Match each visual field defect to its lesion site.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: front = one eye, chiasm = bitemporal, behind = homonymous.

points.p: Optic nerve: monocular vision loss
Optic chiasm: bitemporal hemianopia
Optic tract: homonymous hemianopia
points.why: On the same side as any paresis.

points.p: Occipital cortex: homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

prompts.q: What defects do temporal and parietal lobe lesions cause?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: PITS, and always contralateral.

points.p: Temporal: contralateral superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky')
Parietal: contralateral inferior quadrantanopia ('pie on the floor')
Both are contralateral

prompts.q: Which bitemporal pattern points to a pituitary tumour and which to a craniopharyngioma?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the tumour presses the fibres nearest it first.

points.p: Upper > lower quadrants: compression from below, pituitary tumour
Lower > upper quadrants: compression from above, craniopharyngioma
Craniopharyngioma linked to diabetes insipidus

prompts.q: What causes visual field defects and which presentation is an emergency?

points.p: Stroke, tumour and multiple sclerosis
points.why: The population depends on the cause.

points.p: Sudden homonymous hemianopia: posterior circulation stroke, emergency

prompts.q: What are the complications of a visual field defect?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: speed of treatment decides outcome.

points.p: Reduced quality of life
Permanent vision loss depending on cause and speed of treatment
Driving: must inform the DVLA
points.why: Most homonymous defects fail the field standard.

prompts.q: How do you investigate a visual field defect?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: bedside, then map, then image.

points.p: Bedside confrontation testing first
Formal perimetry maps the defect
MRI brain is the gold standard for the lesion

prompts.q: How is a visual field defect managed?

points.p: Pituitary adenoma with bitemporal hemianopia: trans-sphenoidal surgery
Other tumours: surgery
Stroke: standard stroke pathway
Treat the underlying condition in all cases

prompts.q: Describe the visual pathway from retina to cortex.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: where the fibres cross.

points.p: Retina to optic nerve
Optic chiasm: nasal fibres decussate
points.why: Nasal fibres carry the temporal field.

points.p: Optic tract to lateral geniculate nucleus
points.why: Same half of both eyes travel together.

points.p: Optic radiations (temporal and parietal) to occipital cortex
points.why: Meyer's loop runs in the temporal lobe.

prompts.q: Why do chiasmal lesions cause bitemporal loss, and lesions behind the chiasm homonymous loss?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: crossed versus uncrossed fibres.

points.p: Nasal retinal fibres carry the temporal field and cross at the chiasm
Behind the chiasm fibres from the same side of both eyes travel together

prompts.q: Explain Meyer's loop and macular sparing.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: anatomy explains the sign.

points.p: Meyer's loop (temporal lobe) carries the superior field
Superior radiation (parietal) carries the inferior field
Occipital pole has dual supply: PCA and MCA collaterals
points.why: So the macula is often spared in PCA infarcts.

glossary.visual field: The whole area a person can see while looking straight ahead.
glossary.visual field defect: An area of lost vision within the visual field.
glossary.hemianopia: Loss of half of the visual field.
glossary.bitemporal hemianopia: Loss of the outer (temporal) half of the field in both eyes, from a chiasmal lesion.
glossary.homonymous hemianopia: Loss of the same half (left or right) of the field in both eyes, from a lesion behind the chiasm.
glossary.quadrantanopia: Loss of one quarter of the visual field.
glossary.superior quadrantanopia: Loss of an upper quarter of the field; from a temporal lobe lesion.
glossary.inferior quadrantanopia: Loss of a lower quarter of the field; from a parietal lobe lesion.
glossary.macular sparing: Preserved central vision in a homonymous hemianopia, suggesting an occipital lesion.
glossary.macula: Central part of the retina giving sharp central vision.
glossary.scotoma: A patch of lost vision surrounded by normal vision.
glossary.optic nerve: Carries visual signals from one eye to the chiasm.
glossary.optic chiasm: Where the two optic nerves meet and nasal fibres cross, above the pituitary.
glossary.decussate: To cross to the other side.
glossary.optic tract: Carries fibres from the same half of both retinas from the chiasm to the lateral geniculate nucleus.
glossary.optic radiations: Fibres running from the lateral geniculate nucleus through the temporal and parietal lobes to the occipital cortex.
glossary.Meyer's loop: Lower optic radiation fibres looping through the temporal lobe, carrying the upper visual field.
glossary.PITS: Mnemonic: Parietal Inferior, Temporal Superior quadrantanopias.
glossary.occipital cortex: Primary visual cortex at the back of the brain.
glossary.PCA: Posterior cerebral artery, supplying the occipital lobe.
glossary.MCA: Middle cerebral artery; collaterals help supply the occipital pole.
glossary.confrontation testing: Bedside comparison of the patient's visual field with the examiner's.
glossary.perimetry: Formal machine test that maps the visual field precisely.
glossary.mean deviation: Perimetry summary of how far a field is below normal, in decibels.
glossary.pituitary adenoma: Benign pituitary tumour; large ones compress the chiasm.
glossary.non-functioning: A pituitary tumour that does not secrete excess hormone.
glossary.stalk effect: Mild prolactin rise when a tumour compresses the pituitary stalk and blocks dopamine.
glossary.prolactinoma: Prolactin-secreting pituitary tumour, treated first with dopamine agonists.
glossary.cabergoline: Dopamine agonist used to shrink prolactinomas.
glossary.trans-sphenoidal surgery: Pituitary surgery through the nose and sphenoid sinus.
glossary.craniopharyngioma: Suprasellar tumour, often in children, compressing the chiasm from above.
glossary.suprasellar: Above the sella turcica, where the pituitary sits.
glossary.diabetes insipidus: Lack of ADH action causing large volumes of dilute urine.
glossary.optic neuritis: Inflammation of the optic nerve with painful monocular vision loss, linked to MS.
glossary.MS: Multiple sclerosis: demyelinating disease of the brain and spinal cord.
glossary.posterior circulation stroke: Stroke in the vertebrobasilar territory, including the occipital lobe.
glossary.alteplase: Clot-busting drug used for ischaemic stroke within 4.5 hours.
glossary.thrombolysis: Drug treatment to dissolve a blood clot.
glossary.DVLA: UK Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency; sets visual field standards for driving.
glossary.paresis: Partial weakness of a limb or muscle group.
glossary.atrial fibrillation: Irregularly irregular heart rhythm that can cause embolic stroke.
